speechtext:
Mr. WILFRID GARIEPY (Three Rivers) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend the Interpretation Act.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, nations and families, like individuals, have their red-letter days. Events of special significance call for remembrance. Circumstances of particular importance deserve celebration. It is something of such a nature which prompts me to rise and present this bill.
Short as it is, the purpose of the bill is to recall yearly to our people our independence and emancipation, and to invite them to rejoice over the passage from a state of colony to a state of freedom and liberty. The object of this legislation is to add a holiday to the list of national holidays, and to make such holiday December 11, because the statute of Westminster was adopted in the old land on December 11, 1931.
In rising, I trust and hope to have the support of the house in the move I make. I know this is a request backed and endorsed by our people. I shall not delay proceedings by reading the numerous letters of approval which I have received from persons of different callings, nor shall I read the requests and petitions, the numerous resolutions passed in its favour by all kinds of bodies and societies, the writings of newspapers expressing opinions absolutely in sympathy with it and referring, all of them, to how essential it is for our national welfare that certain anniversaries be blessed and never be allowed to be forgotten by the masses and by the generations to come. This is one of them. Doctor Maurice Ollivier, of the law branch of this parliament has written:
(Translation) The life of all peoples is marked by certain dates which overshadow all others and are as beacons illuminating history and explaining it. In the history of France, it is 1789; in the history of England, 1215, and' in our own history, December 11th, 1931.
(Text) The year 1789 in France meant the end of royalty, the opening of a new era, and a
time when new devices and slogans were inscribed in French laws, and in the constitution of that country.
In England the year 1215 meant the alliance of King John with the nobles of his realm and the birth of that noble document,

Interpretation Act
Magna Charta, more pregnant in its terms and in its objects than anything ever seen before, even in republican Rome or in ancient Greece.
The statute of Westminster is the law par excellence for Canada; it is the crowning gesture in our history; it is the final say in our marvellous advance towards progress, civilization, freedom and world importance. It is achieving the summit, after centuries of struggles and physical and intellectual labours. It is the most important constitutional result secured since the foundation of our country, brought about gradually and progressively by mutual consent, and through the genius displayed by leaders of public opinion.
Representative institutions never existed in this country under the French regime. Absolute monarchy then prevailed, and it may be that such a system was not without some advantages in the pioneering period. Our clergy worked hand in hand with the seigneurs, and truth and gratitude demand that we acknowledge and recognize the services rendered to our different communities then, as well as presently, by our clergy.
The year 1760 changed the flag under which our forefathers lived. In that year was instituted military rule which was not devoid of glory and lustre, but which was unacceptable to a civil population endowed with ambition and self respect.
In 1774 the Quebec Act brought about a slight improvement, an improvement which was still more marked in 1791 under the Constitutional Act, and again under the Union Act of 1840. But it was not until 1848 that, on instructions from the home office to Lord Elgin, the then governor, responsible government came into existence. By their firmness and foresight Lafontaine and Baldwin, giants in statesmanship, obtained from the crown for the Canadian people rights and privileges which cannot be prized too highly. Macdonald and Cartier, with Tupper, Brown, Mowat and others, are the fathers of confederation, as we have it. It is a monument of grandeur, a tower of strength, an instrument of flexible government-imperfect, if you like, but, as events prove, capable of being made suitable to our needs and requirements.
And through it all, from 1760 to 1931 laws and constitutions have been altered in London. There was the supreme power, the final authority. The statute of Westminster, adopted at our request by this final authority, removes every vestige of bondage and makes us sovereign not only within our own walls and frontiers, but throughout the world. Rights of minorities are guaranteed. That which is sacred
remains sacred. But from now on we are a nation, in the full sense of the word; autonomy is firmly and definitely established and consecrated.
I am proud of Canada as she is now, with new rights and responsibilities, and I would say, Let us unite to be great and strong. Let us have not, a condition of province against province, race against race, creed against creed, but a condition where provinces, races and creeds may be standing together in brotherly love, under king and flag, to protect and defend our common heritage.
As a matter of record, may I state briefly the purpose of the statute of Westminster. It is described as "An act to give effect to certain resolutions passed by imperial conferences held in the years 1926 and 1930." It happens to be non-contentious, because we now face the fait accompli. Every political group and party, on behalf of the nation as a whole and without exception, will join in endorsing this great result which, obviously, has had the sanction of the government of the old land.
Doctor Ollivier, who has written extensively on the matter, states that the great war made possible what had looked like a dream before that time. Sixty thousand Canadians died in Flanders. Sir Robert Borden, the then Prime Minister, was emphatic in his views with respect to Canadian representation on post-war settlement commissions and at the meetings of the society of nations.
(Translation) By this statute, writes Mr. Leopold Richer:
. . . the various dominions, including Canada, have become independent countries of the British Empire George VI, is emperor of India.
L'abbe Lionel Groulx has stated:
, kingdoms whose sovereign, also king of England and
This statute is the acknowledgement of a new state of affairs by equals and associates; a political and diplomatic contract drafted and accepted by all, each one speaking and acquiescing in the name of his country with an authority and right absolutely equal to that of the others.
As a preparation to this statute, the imperial conference of 1926 distinctly stated:
Great Britain and the dominions are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
(Text) May I recall that this statute secures for Canada what was desired by the American colonies prior to the Boston tea party. The revolution led by Washington might have been avoided had Lord North been animated by a
Interpretation Act

different spirit. In short, the statute of Westminster declares in a few paragraphs that the British parliament has conferred sovereignty on Canada. Under its terms our country attains majority, is given complete and absolute power. It is liberated from the operation of the Colonial Laws Validity Act and can legislate with extra-territorial effect. It is no more under the power and control of the parliament of the United Kingdom. It is free as far as the merchant shipping act is concerned. The British North America Act is retained just as long as it is desired by ourselves. Amendments to the constitution of Canada are to be in the hands of Canada and Canada only. As it stands now, Canada is to choose its own representatives and make and sign its own'treaties with other nations, untrammeled and without any interference whatsoever. Such conditions have their consequences. Our responsibilities are increased. Being masters in our own home, we must keep a closer eye on everything, not only the constitution itself but on our policies, internal and external. No engagement can bind us unless we are a party to it, and particularly no engagement as to war. This may create the necessity for a truly Canadian flag, the abolition of appeals to the privy council and the immediate attention to sundry matters heretofore attended to outside of our own country.
These are far-reaching changes, of a nature to create pride and self-confidence. Their effect cannot be overestimated, either in time of peace or in time of war. Under the new order of things decisions are not to be binding unless they are arrived at on this side of the water by our own Canadian parliament elected by our people. The genius for government of the British race has never been shown more clearly and established more firmly than by this great move, by this momentous concession of an old and glorious nation to a young and promising people. Rome in its palmy days, like communist Russia, like Italy and like Germany of the present age, believed in force, in armies, in concentration and in domination by sheer power. Not so with the empire of which we are proud to be a part. It is a commonwealth of equal states. Under the statute of Westminster we are partners; we have the same king. But if we bow to the same God and to the same king, nothing can bind us except our own brains, our own conscience, our own choice and decision to select and conclude. In short, His Majesty the King has become the king of Canada, and Canada emerges into complete independence, taking her place under the sun among the free nations of the world.
[Mr. Gariepy.J
Between 1890 and 1900 there was a period of uneasiness in Canada. From Toronto came a demand for imperial federation, whereas in my own province the opposite extremes were advocated, some talking complete independence and others going back to the 1854 bogey and discussing annexation. A satisfactory solution has been found and discord has been replaced by agreement. Men who differed are now united and happy in a common course of thought and action. Deserving of praise and credit as they were in their time, the Quebec Act, the Constitutional Act of 1791, the Union Act and the Confederation Act. although each a step in the right direction, were only moves toward the final and definite evolution which has been reached by the statute of Westminster.
I pray that this house will pass this bill. It is worthy of favourable consideration and enthusiastic approval. I am a Liberal, and I cannot be silent over the fact that the leaders of my party have proved to be no small factors in the adoption of this statute. In a memorable speech Sir Wilfrid Laurier said in a prophetic tone, "Canada is a nation." He gave his life for this country like Thiers, like Gladstone and like Lincoln. Laurier was a martyr to an idea, to an ideal, to a project and to a goal. He wanted all elements and all classes to work in harmony and in agreement so far as Canada's welfare was concerned. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was a disciple of Laurier. He was at the imperial conference of 1926 and history records the stand he took and the lead he gave, ably assisted as he was by his popular Siamese twin, the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). The right hon. Minister of Justice was the first Canadian to sign, in 1923, on behalf of Canada as a free country, a treaty with another nation. It was his glorious lot to impress the British government with the wisdom of this statute when its principles and features were being considered. Just a few days ago he said:
(Translation) In 1929 I had the honour of [DOT]leading a delegation charged with the discussion and preparation of the draft of the statute of Westminster, and I devoted two months to that work.
(Text) Lapointe, Laurier, Cartier, Lafontaine and Papineau-this chain of Quebec leaders in
the political field takes us back to previous centuries and recalls the part played in the progress of this country by the two great predominant races. Justice without favour, peace with honour, protection for one and all-it is under such sound policy that we shall fulfil our duties as Canadian citizens

Interpretation Act
in the enjoyment of a new statute. We shall be true to our king, the king of Canada, but we shall be true also to ourselves. We shall be free like the air we breathe, free as we never were before, thanks to a statute which I want the whole country to salute and be reminded of on December 11 of each year. This is why I present this bill for adoption by this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the hon. member is for the second reading of bill No. 2, to amend the Interpretation Act. I am surprised that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has not risen in his place to declare this bill out of order inasmuch as it involves an expenditure of public money in its printing and in the time of the House of Commons it has taken up at so much per minute. The purpose of this bill is to make a holiday of December 11, which day is to be designated Statute of Westminster day. In my opinion there are too many holidays now, and it would be better if this parliament would devote itself to something practical for the benefit of the working people of this country and of the 300,000 or 400,000 youths who are out of work, rather than taking up time talking about academic questions like the statute of Westminster. This statute has been nothing but an empire wrecking act. It has come near to putting Canada out of the empire. Had it not been for Munich, this statute might have helped to 'bring about the end of the British empire.
We now have as holidays in December, December 9, the king's birthday; December 25, Christmas day, and December 26, which is more or less a holiday. There is also January 1, New Year's day, and it is now proposed to have another holiday, December 11, to be known as Statute of Westminster day. Well, good-bye and good night to work in this country. It is not holidays that the people are looking for; it is remunerative employment in Canada that Canadians want instead of having to go to the United States to look for positions.
Now, as to the proposal of the hon. member: who is asking for this statute?

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE ANNIVERSAEY OP SIGNING OF STATUTE OP WESTMINSTER A STATUTORY HOLIDAY
speechtext: Nobody.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE ANNIVERSAEY OP SIGNING OF STATUTE OP WESTMINSTER A STATUTORY HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Who has petitioned this parliament for a holiday on this date? Let us look at the statute and see what it is. It was the result of what is known as the colonial or imperial conferences-they have changed the name of these meetings-in 1923, 1926 and 1930. The representatives of Canada had no mandate from the Canadian people to
bind us with such a statute as this, and those who went over there did not represent the wisdom and the judgment of the people of this country. Our people were never asked to express an opinion regarding this empirewrecking statute known as the statute of Westminster. Of course, Canada took a leading part in obtaining it. Canada seems always to do all the talking on such matters before these conferences; but when it comes to actual performance paying or doing something practical, she does nothing at all. Canada was responsible very largely for Munich, because she persuaded the mother country to disarm the finest navy, air force and army the world ever saw, with the result that the pacifist pact of Munich was necessarily brought about.
Let us look more closely at this statute, included as chapter 4 in the statutes of Canada, 1932. It is arranged into some twelve sections. It will be noticed, in section 10, that Australia, New Zealand and Newfoundland refused to be associated with this triumph of Canada, the south of Ireland and South Africa, the three dominions which are linked together in this statute. Section 10 states that sections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 of the act shall not apply to Australia, New Zealand or Newfoundland unless they are adopted by those dominions. What are those six sections? They are practically the whole of the binding sections of the statute.
Section 2, relating to the validity of laws made by the parliament of a dominion does not bind Australia, New Zealand or South Africa. It states that:
The Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, shall not apply to any law made after the commencement of this, act by the parliament of a dominion.
The next section relates to the power of parliament to legislate extra-territorially: Canada has adopted that, of course; although she still depends on the British fleet in time of trouble, she is over there leading in the obtaining of this empire-wrecking agreement. By section 4 the parliament of the United Kingdom is not to legislate for a dominion except by its consent. Section 5 deals with the powers of dominion parliaments in relation to merchant shipping. Section 6, as to the powers of dominion parliaments in relation to the courts of admiralty, we also put there.
It is evident that so far as Australia, New Zealand and Newfoundland are concerned, they want to be in the British empire. At this conference it was decided that every dominion must look after its own defence. Canada is coveted by all the dictators because of her magnificent natural resources. With
Interpretation Act

the raw materials that we have, this land would be the happy hunting ground of the dictators if trouble occurred; there is only one agency which separates us from that trouble and from the power of the dictators, and that is the British fleet. The fleet is the protection which the motherland gives this dominion to keep open our trade routes and protect our shores. For that reason I cannot understand such legislation as this. I believe that if this statute had been submitted to the people of Canada, it would have been defeated at the polls. In the elections of 1930 and 1935 I never heard anything about it. Yet it was put over by those interested. In whose interest? To please South Africa and the people of southern Ireland. Australia and New Zealand are excepted from it almost entirely.
Let us go further and see what since this statute came into existence, is the position of the dominions. We will start with the Dominion of Canada, and see how this measure has led to separatism. The story goes back to 1919. I do not assign all-the blame for this to the present government, because some of our own party were connected with this policy a few years ago. They opened a legation at Washington; and if I had been the only Conservative member to do so, I would have voted, had I been here, against the establishment of the Washington legation and other legations all over the seven seas, because in my opinion it was not only fatal in times of peace, but will be most disastrous in time of war. If it had not been for Munich, we would have found that out in twenty-four hours from the dictators. We were near to it during that awful week last September.
What part has Canada played? In 1919 we started this business of separatism by signing the peace treaty at Versailles as a separate nation. I collected these different statutes in an address on a motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) in this chamber on Wednesday, January 27, 1937, and I am reading from my speech in Hansard of that date:
... a separate seat for Canada was demanded and _ secured at the assembly of the League of Nations. In March, 1923, the halibut treaty was signed at Washington by Canada as a separate nation.
I think the present Minister of Justice signed for Canada then.
The imperial conference of 1923 affirmed the right of Canada to sign separate treaties. In 1924 Canada acted separately on the Dawes
glan, and in that year Canada urged that the olonial Laws Validity Act be repealed. In 1926 there was another imperial conference and the right was affirmed of each dominion 
to make separate and independent treaties not binding on any other country. We were given sovereign powers, and we saw the results in the Kellogg note. Separatism has gone far enough in this country. Some would abolish appeals to the privy council; others would abolish the office of lieutenant governor. Many innovations have been made during the last few years, with the result that we have nothing but a policy of separatism in this country, and this resolution, Mr. Speaker, practically says that Canada is a separate country from the mother country, like Spain or Ireland. We are bound to the mother country by ties of loyalty and affection. _ The governor general is also now merely a viceroy and removed from getting any advice from Downing street.
If any advice is required we are now told that Canada is the only place where one can get it. That is the position of Canada. Canada was a party to this statute of Westminster; we signed, sealed and delivered the statute which I spoke of in that debate and which I have just set out.
Now we come to Ireland. The statute was passed to please two dominions, South Africa and the south of Ireland.

speechtext:
Not only has Ireland
abolished the office of governor general and can make its own treaties, but since the passage of this statute the king's head is off the coins and off the postage stamps; there is a separate flag, and the British army has been banished from Ireland. The authority and power for Ireland to act in this fashion were derived from the statute of Westminster. Yet it is supposed to be one of the dominions. From the same source come the powers of the president of Eire, as they call it, or the president of the republic as I call it; others can call it any name they like. Not only that, but Ireland has gone further. She abolished the protection of the motherland so far as the army goes. The Prime Minister of the Irish republic goes over to London and refuses to drink the royal toast at the banquet at the parliament buildings, and then he proceeds to try to annex the Six Counties. That is where they stand under this statute of Westminster.
We come to another of the dominions named in this statute, the Union of South Africa. Where does it stand? That dominion is part and parcel of this statute. On page 1, in the preamble, reference is made to the delegates from the Dominion of Canada, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Dominion of New Zealand, the Union of South Africa, et cetera. The Prime Minister of South Africa refuses to take the privy councillor's oath. They have already hauled down the

Interpretation Act
flag, and they have a little flag of their own in which there is a little eyelet hole for the union jack. The flag which protected them has been removed. They want to follow the example of Ireland, whereby they will want to be outside the empire altogether except for the protection of the British navy, and they appoint their own governor general. They want to be what is called an outside state- outside 364 days in the year, but on the last day wanting the protection of the fleet of the flag that protect their shores. There is no doubt that is where they stand.
Here is a picture of how separatism works. There was a picture in all the Canadian papers away back on November 4, showing Hon. Mr. Pirow, the Minister of Defence of South Africa, reviewing Hitler's troops right in the city of Berlin a week after Munich. And he was there before. What was he doing over there? He was over there to try to get back for Germany by exchange some of her mandated colonies. That is the position to-day; and the right hon. Prime Minister Hertzog has never taken his oath as privy councillor and will not take it. What do we find Hon. Oswald Pirow, Minister of National Defence for the Union of South Africa, doing? He went to Berlin and reviewed Hitler's troops and took the salute. I have a picture in my hand of him reviewing the troops in Berlin. The Union of South Africa some years ago passed an agreement over the head of the mother country whereby certain territories will be given back to Germany in exchange for certain others. The Minister of National Defence for South Africa finally wound up in Great Britain, and what was he trying to do there? Trying to persuade the British government to give Germany back her colonies. In Canada the press, with three or four exceptions, for years have kept the people in the dark by their lip-service to the League of Nations. There are only about four or five newspapers in this country which have opposed this doctrine of separatism.
The Daily Express of Johannesburg has a picture, to which I referred in the debate in this house two weeks ago, of the hauling down of the union jack just before a parade at which General Hertzog took the salute. The caption under the photograph is as follows:
Just before General Hertzog arrived at Swartkop aerodrome to take the salute at to-day's union day parade, officers discovered that the union jack, instead of the union flag, was flying at the saluting base. Hastily they had the union jack hauled down.
That is the position in that dominion.
This doctrine of separatism is disastrous in peace but more futile in war. We saw the
result of it in 1914. Lord Roberts went up and down England telling the people that war was coming, just about a month before war broke out, and he appealed to them and to the dominions for preparedness. The leading statesmen of England, with the exception of Lord Milner, were opposed and would not listen to Lord Roberts, who was telling the people to be prepared. If they had been prepared Great Britain could have bad four hundred thousand troops ready to move at the outbreak of the war, and the war would have been over in a couple of months.
We may have the same state of affairs in Canada as a result of the doctrine of separatism and trying to look after our own defence. Where are we to-day? Suppose Munich had not been a success. Germany's air force has a supremacy in the air estimated at three to one, and they would have been over London within a very few hours. What did the Secretary of State for War in Great Britain, Leslie Hore-Belisha, say? He showed the futility of the defences of London in case of war and gave the people all the real facts, not silence. I quoted in this house a couple of weeks ago what Mr. Chamberlain said that there should be the fullest publicity not only with regard to the defence of England but with regard to Britain's foreign, home and defence policies.
So far as the statute of Westminster is concerned, all the papers of Canada, with five or six exceptions, have been giving lip-service to the League of Nations, hoping that that would save us, that it would provide an armed force to protect our shores. But we know the futility of that hope because the league is done and finished.
There is no demand from the people of Canada for this bill. The act leaves us to look after our own defences ourselves. The explanatory note to the bill states:
Paragraph (11) of section 37 at present reads as follows:
(11) "holiday" includes Sundays, New Year's Day, the Epiphany, Good Friday, the Ascension, All Saints' Day, Conception Day, Easter Monday, Ash Wednesday, Christmas Day, the birthday or the day fixed by proclamation for the celebration of the birthday of the reigning sovereign. Victoria Day, Dominion Day, the first Monday in September, designated Labour Day, Remembrance Day, and any day appointed by proclamation for a general fast or thanksgiving.
Then it goes on to say that the purpose of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Gariepy):
. . . is to make the eleventh day of December a holiday throughout Canada. The Statute of Westminster, which confirmed Canada's present
Interpretation Act

status, that of a sovereign country freely associated as a member of the British commonwealth of nations, was assented to on the eleventh day of December, 1931.
It is fit and proper that this most important anniversary should be kept and observed as a holiday.
The bill is entitled, "An act to amend the Interpretation Act," and reads:
His majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1. Paragraph eleven of section thirty-seven of the Interpretation Act, chapter one of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, as enacted by chapter six of the statutes of 1935, is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(11) holiday' includes Sundays, New Year's Day, the Epiphany, Good Friday, the Ascension, All Saints' Day, Conception Day, Easter Monday, Ash Wednesday, Christmas Day, the birthday or the day fixed by proclamation for the celebration of the birthday of the reigning sovereign, Victoria Day, Dominion Day, the elevfnth day of December, designated Statute of Westminister Day, the first Monday in September, designated Labour Day, Remembrance Day, and any day appointed by proclamation for a general fast or thanksgiving;"
I see no demand for this legislation, Mr. Speaker. But this government wants to change everything.
Under the statute of Westminster each of the dominions is to be responsible for its own home defence. Where is Canada's? What home defence have we if Canada is invaded by the dictators? We had a little discussion in this house last year about Japan-

speechtext:
I must congratulate the hon.
member for Three Rivers (Mr. Gariepy) on his very fine address and thank him personally for his kind words concerning myself. I hope he will not be too disappointed if I question the necessity or the opportuneness of carrying the bill into legislation. The hon. member for Three Rivers said such nice things about the modest work I had to do in connection with what led to the statute of Westminster that I needed the other words of my hon. friend the member for Broadview (Mr. Church) to bring me down to a status of humility.
As far as the proposal is concerned, to declare this particular date a holiday, to attain the purpose of the proposer of the bill would need more amendments than this one, because the Interpretation Act only defines what a holiday is when there is no other interpretation in the text of special legislation. On every occasion when we celebrate a holiday, that holiday is defined. For instance, in the Bank Act, in the Letters of Exchange Act, in the Civil Service Act, the holidays provided for are therein all described; and merely to add this date to the Interpretation Act would not have the effect of creating holidays for the various purposes of those legislative enactments. That could be remedied, of course, by adding amendments to the bill. I am doubtful, however, about the proposal itself, not because of the motives of my hon. friend but because I believe that

Interpretation Act
*
the first of July, Dominion day, is the national day of Canada and embraces the commemoration of all that Canada has done in her progress to nationhood.
Dominion day means confederation day. The confederation was formed in 1867 by the joining together of four colonies, and the new nation, or at least the country that was on the way to nationhood, gradually added to itself other provinces and made various improvements to reach the status which we now enjoy. This has been a gradual process. I will not describe the various stages; my hon. friend did. The year 1926, of course, crystallized the work that had been done, and the position of Canada in the British commonwealth was actually defined and accepted by all on a status of equality. In 1929 we had the conference in London where a draft of the statute of Westminster was prepared, discussed, debated and accepted and finally, in the following year, the statute was enacted defining Canada's nationhood.
All along there were many difficulties to be met and faced. Every step forward has been fought, most frequently by arguments such as those used by the hon. member for Broadview to-night. I may say that even those who accept the statute of Westminster to-day, and not only accept it but celebrate its anniversary on different occasions, were rather indifferent at the time, and some of them were apprehensive. It was represented as meaning separatism, separation from the British empire, as the hon. member for Broadview said to-night. Of course, it is the opposite. It is a symbol of union; it is unity and freedom; it is the bond that binds together the various parts of the commonwealth under the same crown. Freedom is the cement that binds all these nations together, and if the people of Canada and of the various countries of the commonwealth had ideas such as those expressed by the hon. member for Broadview, that, I believe, would lead to division, disunion and disruption.
Fortunately, my hon. friend's voice is one in the wilderness, because most of the people of Canada accept the situation as it is and are pleased at the change. But-and here I address myself to the hon. member for Three Rivers-the statute of Westminster applies to all Canada. It was the goal of all Canada and Dominion day, which is Canada's day, the national day of the whole country, embraces it all; so that undoubtedly the celebration of Dominion day, the Westminster act and the statute that was passed as a result of that act, all go together.
I do not believe that too many holidays would be advisable. I believe perhaps we ought to have fewer holidays, but we should celebrate them with greater keenness, more fervour and more patriotic enthusiasm. For instance, Dominion day, Canadian day, is not in my opinion celebrated as it should be throughout the country as the national day, as the national days of other nations are celebrated. It should be more assertive of the national spirit of Canada. I repeat, I do not think there should be too many holidays.
I have a list of the public holidays in England. For instance, bank holidays in England and Wales, Ireland and the Channel islands are, Easter Monday, Whit-Monday, the first Monday in August and the first day after Christmas or Boxing day. Banks are also closed on Good Friday and Christmas day; stock exchanges are closed on bank holidays; customs houses and docks are also closed on bank holidays and the king's birthday, June 3, or when decreed. It appears that the banks are open on the king's birthday, because it i3 specially stated that customs houses and docks are celebrating the same holidays as the banks, with the addition of the king's birthday. The law offices close on Good Friday, Easter Monday and Tuesday, Whit-Monday, Christmas day and the first day after Christ-' mas, that is Boxing day. There are really less holidays there than we have here at the present time.
I have another reason to offer. The statute of Westminster is a great step; but it is not as final for Canada as it has been for most of the other dominions, because of certain things which prevent complete nationhood, in spite of the fact that those obstacles are of our own will, are there because we want them to be there.

I have
only five minutes left, and I may be presumptuous, but what I have to say is more important to me than giving the statement that my hon. friend would like me to make.
First, there is the right to amend our own constitution. This is the most important legislative work; it is our own charter; the conditions under which we act as legislatures here and in the provinces are still laid down at Westminster. This is by our own desire, because of our special conditions, but it is there. How can it be accepted in international law
Interpretation Act

*
that we are a fully sovereign nation when we have to resort to the parliament of another country to effect changes in our constitutional structure? This creates a situation which 1 hope to take the opportunity to deal with in connection with some important matters which will be debated this session concerning foreign affairs and various bills which are on the order paper.
In the second place, there are the privy council appeals. There, again, it is our own will; we can change it any time; we have the right to abolish appeals to the privy council, but we have not done so. Litigants from Canada must go to the mother country to get a final decision in Canadian cases. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said last year, the sovereignty of Canada resides in the judicial committee.
There is another matter which has been discussed this session for a couple of hours, but which seems to be treated as futile, namely, the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag. We cannot say that we have complete equality of status and full sovereignty until we have a Canadian flag. As far as I am concerned-I am speaking only for myself- I think the three matters I have mentioned will have to be dealt with and definitely solved before we can say that we are like the other dominions which have all done so. These dominions are as loyal as Canada, their people as loyal as any Canadians. But there are some people in Canada with the ideas of the hon. member for Broadview, who are afraid of asserting themselves, or to declare that they are full Canadian citizens.
This is not in any respect talking in favour of separation. I tell hon. members most sincerely and earnestly that I believe that the best way to keep the Dominion of Canada in the British commonwealth of nations-I hope to God it will always remain in the British commonwealth of nations-is to have a Canada free and equal in status in every respect. It is cooperation in freedom. And I repeat, none of those steps has led or will lead to separation.
I am pleased that my hon. friend has brought the matter up, in order that it might be discussed; it is an important subject. I do not suppose he expected that his bill would be accepted this session. His purpose must have been accomplished by having the matter discussed, and I suppose he will not insist on his bill being enacted this year.

And I am repeating it tonight. The government may be right in adopting this policy, but personally I do not think they are. I believe they are not looking far enough ahead, and I believe they have drifted into their policy as the easiest course to follow in the recent emergency, instead of taking a long-range view, instead of realizing that we are really just beginning this business of defending ourselves and that / we shall require munitions and war equipment for many many years to come.
Australia has gone the other way. She has an arsenal policy, developed after the war- which is the time, incidentally, when Canada should have developed her defence policy.. And the House of Commons might very well remember that during all those years the present Prime Minister was at the head of the Canadian government.
After the war Australia set out on an effective arsenal policy. The result is that she produces not only her own munitions, but also her own machine guns and rifles, and I believe she either produces or is able to produce her light artillery and anti-aircraft guns, and her 4-5 howitzers. Defence Purchasing Board
in 1935 and 1936. I think it should be noted that the sixth recommendation by that commission is as follows:

At the present time the civil servants, most of them, have no respect for their ministers, and why? The debates that have been going on for a month or so now may, after all, prove to have served a most useful purpose. There were similar debates in Great Britain during the early days of the war and we had them here too. It brought about here a demand for reforms.
There are a few things which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. The resolution declares that it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a defence purchasing board with exclusive power, sub-, ject to approval of the governor in council, to enter into all contracts for the purchase of munitions and so forth in cases where the expenditure exceeds $5,000. In my opinion it would be better for the new board to assume complete control, with the necessary safeguards, over contracts amounting to more than $200, not only over those of more than $5,000. That was more or less the policy during the war, and competitive bids were called for those up to $200. Over that there would be a straight contract under the board.
I hope that the minister will see to it that everyone who wishes to have his plant surveyed will be given that opportunity. Prior to the war the Baldwin interests had a granite sets plant in Toronto at Ashbridge bay. In the early days of the war tariff changes were made which handicapped it, and it was at last turned into one of the largest munition factories in the empire. It was under the control of the British munitions board. The first shipment of shells, only a few, was made in December, 1914, and in 1915, on the institution of a new policy of the British munitions board, production went ahead by leaps and bounds. The late Mr. Fred Miller, a great

Defence Purchasing Board

patriot, was connected with the plant in an honorary way, as was also Mr. E. L. Cousins, manager of the harbour board. As I say, it was one of the largest munitions establishments in the British empire and it did very well.
I wish this new board every success, and I do not believe that the discussion which has taken place in this house, and which, after all, led to and was responsible for a board, will do any harm, because it will be aa intimation to the manufacturers of Canada that they must be up and doing. The Economist of London, England, has had some pertinent remarks to make with regard to the question of home defence. I quote:
It is not merely with reluctance, but with repugnance that most citizens acquiesce in rearmament. There is one aspect of the matter, however, to which these feelings need not so fully apply. The army the navy, and the air force are each of them necessarily concerned with the taking of life and the destruction of wealth. But there is a fourth arm, home defence, which, though it costs money which can ill be spared, is at least concerned exclusively with protection and preservation. Home defence, moreover, has a peculiar urgency for Great Britain, for in many ways we are one of the most vulnerable of European nations. It is more difficult for us than for others either to protect our population from air raids or to ensure that they are supplied with food.
I .trust that the new organization which is to be set up will follow the principles and great record that guided the British munitions board in Canada during the great war. When the war broke out Canada did not have a single plant to make shells, but by the cooperation of manufacturers, of labour and of a large number of key men who served voluntarily and without pay, a glorious record was made by Canada, and I wish the minister's new board equal success.
Iron and steel are the principal ingredients in modern armaments. Let me read two paragraphs from the report by the imperial munitions board of what Canada did; and I hope this new board will be able to parallel those achievements. In the report issued by the British war cabinet for the year 1917 it was stated:
Canada's contribution during the last year has been striking. Fifteen per cent of total expenditure of the ministry of munitions in the last six months of the year was incurred in that country. She has manufactured nearly every type of shell from 18 pounder to 9-2 inch. In the case of the 18 pounder no less than 55 per cent of the output of shrapnel shells in the last six months came from Canada, and most of these were complete rounds of ammunition. .	.	. Canada also contributed
42 per cent of the total 4-5 inch shells, 27 per cent of the 6 inch shells, 20 per cent of the 8 inch and 16 per cent of the 9'2 inch.

The following figures give some idea of what Canada accomplished in the production of munitions of war:

1915		 57,213,688
1916		 296,505,257
1917		 388,213,553
1918		 260,711,751
The report continues:
The effect of the establishment of the munitions industry in Canada in increasing iron and steel production is also observable in the statistics of manufactures. In 1915 the iron and steel products industry of Canada produced commodities to the value of $120,422,420, while in 1917 its products were valued at $400,385,086, and in 1918 at $443,455,779. The chemical and allied products industry was also greatly stimulated by the war. Commodities to a gross value of $45,410,486 were produced by this industry in 1915 while in 1917 the gross value increased to $133,618,658 and in 1918 the gross products were valued at $173,649,073.
That is the glorious record of this dominion, considering it had at the beginning no factories and no industry to manufacture shells.
The manager of the British munitions board in Canada was David Carnegie, C.B.E., formerly member and ordnance adviser, shell committee, and imperial munitions board, Ottawa. He has given an account of the history of munition supplies in Canada, and I hope the new board will follow the great example in business administration which that board gave.
The former Prime Minister of Great Britain, Right Hon. David Lloyd George, shows what Canada has done. He says:
Though the material required could not then be produced in Canada, for, it must be remembered, no private manufacturer had ever made a shell in that country and the output of the only arsenal need not be considered, the Canadian manufacturers, under the initiative and leadership of the Minister of Militia, produced these munitions.
Then the account goes on to refer to the fact that the contract was for 220,000 shells a week but owing to the organization of the board they produced 400,000 18-inch shrapnel shells, twice the number called for in the contract.
Mr. Winston Churchill at the conclusion of the war wrote a letter of congratulation to the board for the great work it had done.
Then the United States came into the war, and it was fortunate for that country that Canada had the British munitions board. Let me read just two paragraphs concerning that:
In the autumn of 1917, after the government of the United States entered the war, negotiations were opened between the officials of the United States ordnance department and the Imperial Munitions Board, with a view to placing at the disposal of the United States the surplus forgings and machining capacity which had been developed in Canada.

Defence Purchasing Board
At the time in question Canada had a shellforging and machining capacity for 18 pounder shells of 400,000 per week, and had actually shipped overseas 32,000,000 of these shells. This remarkable development had taken three years' hard work and organization but now was not fully required by the British government, who had increased her manufacturing capacity in Great Britain. The actual requirements of the British government from Canada amounted to 150,000 to 200,000 per week, leaving an unused capacity of 200,000 to 250,000. It was this latter capacity the Imperial Munitions Board on behalf of the manufacturers of Canada, and in the interest of the Allies, placed at the disposal of the United States government. The proposal was opportune, as at the time the United States were making desperate efforts to organize for the production of the 75 mm. high explosive shells. This shell was about the same size as the British 18 pounder shells. It was therefore with the object of assisting the United States ordnance department in carrying out its munitions program that negotiations were begun.
So we see what was done in Canada by all the parties uniting in harmony. I hope that the new board will go to work and that not only shall we get orders from our own defence department for home defence but that Canada will have a large share of the munition orders of the mother country in her rearmament, because we are not getting it now. In addition, I hope that advancement will be made all along the line and that Canada will be making the record for itself which it made in the late war.

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Power for the second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Pension Act.

subtopic: ABOLITION OF PENSION APPEAL COURT AND EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PENSION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Before the bill passes its second reading, I have a few observations to make. I wish to associate myself very warmly with the remarks made last evening by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). I am not' in opposition to the bill. I think the minister is to be commended for proposing to abolish the pension appeal court and to set forward the date for receipt of applications for pensions.
I think, before the bill passes second reading, the minister should take an opportunity to explain to the house his attitude with regard to several important proposals which have been made to him by organized ex-service men in connection with pensions. An honest endeavour was made earlier in this parliament to recast as it were the Pension Act and to bring all pension matters to a stage of finality. Since that time we have experienced various problems; we have encountered several anomalies in the act; and I think that on this occasion, when he is introducing an amending bill, a further effort should be made to bring to a stage of finality these important problems with regard to which the minister has received recommendations.
I do not wish my remarks to be construed as opposition to the bill introduced by the minister, but this is the only opportunity we shall have to point out its inadequacies and to invite him to make a pronouncement with regard to several matters which should be dealt with at this time.
I am of the opinion that a bill of this kind should be referred to a special committee of the house. There are several important and valid reasons why it should be dealt with by a special committee. This matter of pensions should be considered with relation to the general problem. If it becomes possible to deal with small groups under the Pension Act without violating the principles of that act, that, I think, should be done with relation to existing problems among ex-service men. The question of pensions is a subject of a highly technical nature, and can be discussed more readily and with more facility in a special committee. A committee provides a useful forum for the receipt of recommendations and the discussion of them without
detaining or unduly occupying the time of the house. Furthermore, it is important with regard to the pensions question, with the experience we now have, that we should bring this matter, as I have said before, to the stage of finality.	.
I think it is important that the minister should make a pronouncement at this time with regard to the claim of non-pensioned widows. This matter has received considerable attention in recent months, and certain classifications of those widows have a strong claim upon the government and upon this country. I believe a strong case can be made for those widows of ex-service men who until the time of death were in receipt of pensions. Those women up to the time of their husbands' deaths were in receipt of the additional pension. They were in a sense assured up to the time of death of an income in respect of the disability incurred during service. Because it cannot be definitely established that the man's death was due to a pensionable disability, they are cut off with, perhaps, only a month's allowance. I think consideration should be given to those in that classification who are in destitute circumstances, who were in receipt of the additional pension until the time of death of their husbands and that some form of allowance on the basis of need should be extended to those widows to enable them to adjust themselves to a new mode of life. After all, if they are in destitute circumstances they must apply for relief, either for mothers' allowance or some other form of aid, to the provincial or civic authority, and usually the federal government contributes a large proportion of the assistance extended to them. I think they have a just and proper claim upon the federal government. There would be no great expenditure involved. As far as I can ascertain by an examination of the departmental figures, not a very large number are involved in that classification, and I believe that at this stage the government would be well advised in moving forward to a sympathetic consideration of this classification.
With regard to the other classifications, I think some of them at least might be placed on the same basis as the widows of those who were in receipt of war veterans' allowance at the time of death, and who at the present time receive the allowance for the continued period of twelve months. Much could be said in this regard. I am confident that already, because of representations made to him, the.minister must have given the matter careful attention.
Perhaps I should refer to these cases where there is doubt, the borderline cases
179S
Pension Act Amendment

where it may be contended strongly that the pensionable disability was a contributing factor to death. I have under my hand a copy of a decision made by the pension appeal court which I think illustrates the point I am discussing at *the moment, where a man had established entitlement to pension, where he was admitted to hospital because he required operative treatment-he was pensionable for a chest condition-and as a result of the administration of a general anaesthetic he developed bronchial pneumonia and death ensued within a few days. In this particular case the appeal court went to considerable trouble to question the former decision rendered by the pension commission with regard to entitlement. The deceased officer in question happened to have had service in the British forces. It was shown in the concluding paragraph of the judgment that there was doubt, even in the minds of the members of the pension appeal court who signed the judgment, and by the way, the case was appealed by the crown. The court felt that a further claim should be made and that it might be possible in their opinion to consider fresh evidence with regard to entitlement. I feel that cases of this kind should be again reviewed, under the new and amended legislation, by the pension commission. I think that in cases such as this a powerful contention may be made for some form of allowance to the widow who is not now pensionable and because a reasonable doubt exists that the pensionable disability was a contributing factor to death. In this case the widow had some assurance that because of her husband's disability she would receive some form of income from the state with respect to that disability. Certainly in many of these cases the widow during her husband's life gave the best years of her own life irr administering to his comfort and need when the man was handicapped by his war disability.
I wish again to stress the necessity of amending the legislation dealing with the needs of those suffering from mental and nervous disorders. That ground was traversed last evening by the hon. member for Vancouver South, and I support him in that regard. I suppose that almost every hon. member is having considerable trouble with claims advanced by men suffering from some form of neurological disorder. I have under my hand a case which, I believe, illustrates the point

a man who had three enlistments and who gave meritorious service in France. There is a record of hospitalization, while on [.Mr. MacNeil.] '
active service, for epilepsy, mania and neurasthenia. Nevertheless, upon examination by the neuro-psychiatrists of the treatment branch, it was diagnosed that he was suffering from psychopathic personality of constitutional origin, that there was superimposed on that psychopathic personality an anxiety neurosis, and to quote the report:
On the strength of the neurological report and diagnosis to psychopathic personality, the commission have ruled that the entire disability present in this case is the result of the constitutional condition and psychopathic personality with spasmodic affection of the eye, and the man's award of pension previously paid at 30 per cent for anxiety neurosis lias been discontinued.	.
I have no criticism in this regard of the pension commission, 'but the man's total disability was thirty per cent. He is receiving pension for aggravation at the rate of eighteen per cent because of the spasmodic affection of the eye. I suggest that if section 11 (b) be suitably amended by the house at this time along the line suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South, the pension commission would be on stronger ground in dealing with these cases and be in a position to relieve the worry and anxiety which these men are occasioned, and which I contend accentuates rather than removes their disability. That is in my opinion an important matter. I believe it was the original intention of parliament to protect the man who served in a theatre of actual war with regard to pre-enlistment disability. It was never intended that there should be discrimination in respect of mental or nervous disorders. I fail to comprehend why there should be any distinction drawn between, say tuberculosis, and a mental disorder. If a man had any constitutional or hereditary tendency to pulmonary tuberculosis, no discrimination is made because of that, and upon discharge from the service he is given the full protection of this section of the act. But by reason of the recommendations of the neuropsychiatrists of the treatment branch, who dominate the situation with respect to diagnosis, this discrimination against mental or nervous disorders does exist to-day, and a certain number of men, whether the number be large or not I do not know, are suffering grievous hardship as a result. I urge upon the minister that he take the opportunity of amending the act in the way previously suggested, so that men in this category may be given their full rights.
I find that this bill makes no provision for the plight of those dealt with under section 77 of the Pension Act, and that also was referred to last evening-the payment of

Pension Act Amendment
additional pension in respect of children born after May 1, 1933. I would remind the house that this section was introduced as an economy measure when the depression was at its depth, and no longer is there any good reason for the maintenance of this section.
I also urge that the date with respect to marriage contracted subsequently to the appearance of disability, which is now January, 1930, should be moved forward to synchronize with the final date for payment of additional pensions, May 1, 1933, or delete section 77; in one way or the other remove the apparent anomaly that exists in the Pension Act.
I again urge upon the minister the necessity of dealing more generously with the nonpensionable widow. If he cannot see his way clear to assuming any additional responsibility in this respect at the present time, he should at least give consideration to lowering or extending the classification. At the present time provision is made for the dependents of those who died in receipt of pensions, classes 1 to 5. That might be lowered to include those in receipt of fifty or sixty per cent pension without incurring any great additional liability, and again meeting the need of those who are rendered dependent by death where the pensionable disability is a contributing factor to death.
I do not wish to detain the house at length.
I merely urge upon the minister at this stage that he make a declaration on behalf of the government with regard to the important recommendations which have been advanced and which should now receive consideration.
I repeat my suggestion that it would be proper at this time to have a brief inquiry by a special committee of the house where all these technical matters might be adequately and frankly discussed to the satisfaction of the organized ex-service men.
Hon. H. II. STEVENS (Kootenay East): Mr. Speaker, this bill, of course, is strictly limited. I gather that it deals merely with the change from the appeal court to appeal boards of the commission.
I am inclined to agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), who has just taken his seat, that it might be advisable to set up again this session a special committee to deal with the numerous, and, I think, reasonable requests, many of them, that have been made by veterans' organizations. I recall that over the years since the war, the special committees that have been set up from time to time to deal with soldier problems have done extremely valuable work. I think all who know of the work of those 71492-114
special committees will agree with me in paying tribute to the splendid work done by the present minister (Mr. Power) when he was a private member of the house and a member of that committee, and, on some occasions, chairman of it.
While I was not a member of that committee, I do recall that few committees of this house have carried on their deliberations with a more genuine spirit of cooperation, or reported to the house with a greater degree of unanimity than the special committee which was set up from time to time to deal with pensions and returned soldier problems. I suggest that at this session a similar committee should again be set up, to which this bill might be referred, for the purpose, not of dealing with this particular subject but, rather, of reviewing the position of the veterans as it is to-day.
I am quite aware that there will naturally be in the minds of many people the thought that sooner or later wTe must call a halt on pension legislation. But I feel that this concept is not a very sound one in the light of the facts with which we are confronted at the present time.
May I now turn the thoughts of the members of the house for a short time in a slightly different direction. From time to time we are told, as, for instance, when we were dealing with the question of free hospitalization or free medical attendance of a civilian nature, that these, are matters of provincial jurisdiction where the province must be considered, and where, indeed, our jurisdiction is distinctly questioned. And so again with questions of relief. We are told that this is primarily a municipal matter, certainly a provincial matter, but that through grants in aid we can cooperate. But the welfare of veterans is definitely and distinctly a federal responsibility, and I think the time has arrived when we as a parliament ought clearly to declare, as we have in a half-hearted way declared at times in the past, that this is a federal matter and that we propose definitely to take that responsibility on our shoulders. I think if we should so declare, it would go a long way toward clearing the atmosphere.
I am not giving to the house anything new when I refer to a document issued by the Canadian Legion containing a copy of an address by the late Sir Robert Borden when he was Prime Minister. I have no doubt members of the house are familiar with it, and I shall not quote it at length but rather refer to it for the purpose of supporting what I have just said. In this address by Sir Robert

Pension Act Amendment

Borden to the members of the Canadian expeditionary force in 1917, I find the following language:
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion that the country will support the government to prove to the returned men its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire, and that no man, whether he, goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died.
These were magnificent words spoken by the then Prime Minister of Canada, and in my opinion-and I have always held this view tenaciously-it was a declaration that we dare not break faith with those men, a declaration which we must respect. Taking that view, I hold that we should not hesitate to declare that it is our federal responsibility, the responsibility of this parliament, to care for the veterans of the great war. What does that involve? I know that we cannot respond to all the requests and suggestions, because many of these requests, though made by men in good faith, are made without an appreciation of the magnitude of the demands or of their seriousness-demands such as a large bonus to every individual, and so on. Some of these requests cannot be entertained, but the least that parliament can do is, as we have done in the past, from time to time to review the general conditions of the veterans of the last war, in such a manner as to ensure that we are doing the maximum in caring for them.
There is a second point I wish to emphasize. The other day we spent several hours discussing state medicine, and it has been discussed on several occasions in this house. Well, there should be no hesitancy on the part of parliament in assuming responsibility for the complete hospitalization of the veterans of the last war, irrespective of whether they are pensionable or not. I speak now as a layman and from observation and contact with these men, and while of course my opinion is not technically authoritative, it is nevertheless my view that most of these men are probably eight or ten years older than they are, if I might use that contradiction in terms. By virtue of that service they are aged before their time. I may be wrong, but that is my impression. I meet men I know who are no older than myself, but they are certainly much older in their physical condition than I am, and I think that is generally the case. For that reason we ought frankly to accept the responsibility of hospitalization for the

veterans, and I would make no discrimination regarding the causes of their illness, and so on. I would accept responsibility in the name of the people of Canada, and because I think parliament must keep faith with the declaration made by the Prime Minister of Canada of that time, with full knowledge and a sense of responsibility of his statement as Prime Minister, that we would take care of these men.
The hon. member for Vancouver North referred to the question of widows' pensions. I am not sufficiently acquainted with the technique of this subject, the particulars of the law, to discuss it, nor do I wish to discuss it at length. But there in that connection is a point which I think we could well take into consideration. The widow of a veteran, although for pension purposes, under the law as at present drafted she may not be entitled to continuation of the pension, because of lateness of marriage or for some other reason, is nevertheless in my opinion still entitled to special consideration by this parliament, and I again apply to that subject the same test I applied to the other, namely, that we are called upon in Canada, through the provinces and the municipalities, to care for the derelict, the unfortunate, the unemployed and the destitute citizens of the country, by tens of thousands. We do that with the question of jurisdiction constantly thrust forward, whereas we have here a group whom we might very well take under our care, and the responsibility for whom this dominion should assume.
There is another question which is perhaps more difficult. I do not admit that in these two other instances I have mentioned, the question of hospitalization of veterans and the question of widows, there is any complicated difficulty. But the next is perhaps a little more complicated, and that is as regards imperial veterans resident in Canada. With respect to this class, I recognize, of course, that there may be two broad divisions. On the one hand there is the imperial veteran who is perhaps an old country born man, who enlisted in the early weeks or months of 1914 in the imperial army. Many of them hastened away because of the delay at Valcartier and because they wanted to get back and join the imperial forces. At any rate, they left Canada and joined the imperial forces, and they are naturally subject to such benefits as the imperial parliament may have granted. There is a technical argument- that can be advanced regarding this class, and that is that they are imperial veterans and that therefore the imperial parliament must take care of them. On many occasions since the

Pension Act Amendment
war their rights or requests have been reviewed, and we did make certain concessions, so that the answer I have just indicated does not really hold good. I say, we have made certain concessions to them. Now I suggest that their requests should be again reviewed by a competent committee of the house to consider whether or not we could extend to them some additional privileges which they do not now enjoy. I suggest that we might very well include them in the privileges of free hospitalization. These are certain major questions to which I wanted to refer.
There is, of course, the question of taking care of or making what we call economic provision for the returned unemployed. I hold in my hand a letter which I received from the Cranbrook branch of the Canadian Legion, signed by its secretary, W. S. Johnston. from which I quote one paragraph:
The officers and members of the branch are in complete sympathy -with the proposal that the dominion government adopt the principle contained in the recommendation of the veterans' assistance commission and the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion at Fort William; "that unemployed ex-service men who saw service in the theatre of actual war be paid a provisional economic allowance by the dominion government while unemployed."
That is a suggestion made not only by this branch but by the veterans' association and the Canadian Legion generally. I am quite aware that it might be argued that the federal authorities should not be asked to pay an allowance to unemployed veterans. But we are caring for our unemployed-this is a point I should like to emphasize-and some at least suggest that many of the unemployed are now getting substantial relief, and more than is granted under the soldiers' aid provision. In other words, the civil unemployed get from the civic authorities plus the dominion grant more than do veterans directly from the department. I again submit that inasmuch as we are called upon to make very heavy grants to the provinces and the municipalities on general unemployment, this is a section of our citizens that we might well consider taking under our special and direct care.
Many of these men are, because of war service, burnt-out before their time. I am sure medical men in the house will support me when I say that because of war service many of these men who are unemployed or only partly employed, are not employable in the ordinary sense of the term. A great many of them are, as a result of their war service, quite unfit for ordinary manual labour. I know that in some instances men who suffered 71492-114i
some slight wound or sickness overseas, some of the very best of them, did not report or disclose their disability or sickness during service; when they came back from the war they felt fairly good and they said-some of them used pretty frank language-"To the devil with it; I am not going to bother about pension or make any application," so they just let it slide, and the record is gone. Now, as these men have grown older, it is difficult for medical men to determine whether their present disability is exactly due to war service.
It is true we have in the law a provision referring to the burnt-out group and borderline cases, but the law has been fairly strictly interpreted. The minister rather smiles; perhaps he thinks I am wrong in that, but I know cases where it has been strictly interpreted. I cannot of course speak for a very large number; but within my own knowledge there have been many cases that I have brought to the attention of the authorities, and in some instances they have been adjusted. Perhaps it was because I and others pressed the matter, not in any political sense; the minister and the department under the present administration will react just the same as any others, but in many instances there has been an adjustment, or shall I say justification of an adjustment has been recognized, after reviews which it was difficult to get and which had been denied in the ordinary interpretation of the law. That being so, I say we should take responsibility for these cases and recognize them definitely as a federal responsibility.
I wish also to refer to another communication which I received only a day or two ago from the Canadian veterans' bonus league at Regina, signed by its president, Mr. Cole, and its secretary, Mr. Gee. I shall not read the whole communication, but it impresses me as a rather reasonable analysis of the case. I quote a paragraph or two-

speechtext:
There may be differences of opinion among ex-service men, but I never allow that to interfere with my approach to
Pension Act Amendment

this question. I think we should approach the question in a very broad spirit. This letter contains this paragraph:
We contend that the soldier of 1914-18 served the nation as a whole and no section in particular; that during such service he was a complete charge-
This is rather a good argument; I would like the minister to catch it.
-he was a complete charge of the federal government during the time of service, therefore as a veteran should still be such a charge, and that the federal government should assume the full responsibility for their welfare.
I think that is putting the matter succinctly and well. Then they make certain suggestions. They asked for action during the present session to cover these points-I will read the points as they have outlined them:
1.	Place the responsibility for the care of the veterans where it rightfully belongs, on the federal government.
With that I entirely agree.
2.	Deal with the problems of that class of veteran that is incapable of competition in the labour market due to age and disability.
3.	Create Work and employment for this class of veteran that will be of a permanent nature and not that type of employment which will be discontinued in a few *weeks or months and then place the veteran back where he is.
4.	In ordering certain types of employment for the exclusive employment of veterans over a period of years guarantee permanency and allowing the veteran to stabilize his economic position.
5.	Give the Canadian veterans certain preferences over imperial veterans.
Well, I have never argued that we should place the imperial veterans in exactly the same position as Canadian veterans. I think it is a question that is open to argument. I think we should be very generous towards the imperial veteran in any of these measures of assistance that we can render, particularly if he was long a resident of Canada before the war, as many of them were. Many of them were born here; others were men who had lived in the country a good many years. I know one little village, Wallashee on the Canadian Pacific main line near Ashcroft, B.C., where there were twenty-seven ablebodied men when the war broke out. Every man went and went immediately. They had been in that village for years building up little fruit ranches. As you go by you can see these ranches to-day, gone to waste, the fruit trees dead and the neat little houses now
[Mr. Stevens. 1
a wreck. Not one man lived. The whole village was wiped out. That is the class of men they were. Of those who did fortunately come back, many had spent years in building up the country and are entitled to such consideration as I have suggested.
There are a number of other points to which I might refer, but I see it is eleven o'clock. I suggest earnestly to the minister that a committee be set up this session to review the present requests and suggestions for dealing with the veterans, and that parliament should declare at this session that it accepts the responsibility of caring for the veterans of the great war as a definite and distinct responsibility.
